paragraphs: Removing targeted knowledge from a language model becomes harder when removal requests arrive repeatedly. Each update can damage useful capabilities, so successive unlearning tasks may compound that damage. This paper studies continual unlearning, focusing on how to remove unwanted knowledge while retaining the model’s broader usefulness.

The proposed method, ALKN, builds on a task vector framework and concentrates updates through dynamic masking. The mask makes training gradients sparse, restricting which parameters receive changes instead of broadly modifying the model. ALKN also adjusts the strength of unlearning according to relationships between tasks. These mechanisms address both where an update acts and how strongly it acts as the sequence of removal tasks develops.

Across three established unlearning datasets, the authors report consistently better unlearning effectiveness and utility retention than baseline methods in continual settings. The findings support selective, adaptive updates as a way to manage repeated removal requests. They show improvements on both evaluation goals, rather than treating stronger forgetting alone as evidence of successful unlearning.
icml-2025-adaptive-localization-of-knowl.tldr: ALKN selectively updates parameters and adapts unlearning strength to improve repeated knowledge removal while retaining useful capabilities.

paragraphs: Preference optimization trains a language model to favor responses people prefer. The paper identifies two difficulties in existing approaches: DPO keeps a static reference model as the policy changes, while SimPO uses the same target reward margin for examples with different preference strengths. AlphaDPO makes the reference distribution and resulting margins adaptive.

Its implicit reference combines a uniform distribution with a powered ratio between the current policy and the original reference. This construction balances policy-driven specialization with uniform exploration and allows the reward margin to vary by instance. The authors also prove that the method implicitly controls the KL divergence between successive policy updates, providing a theoretical basis for stability even when reference models are poorly calibrated.

Experiments across Mistral2-7B, Llama3-8B, and Gemma2-9B report state-of-the-art results, including a 58.7% length-controlled win rate on AlpacaEval 2 and a 35.7% win rate on Arena-Hard. The reported alignment gains do not require multi-stage training. Together, the theory and experiments support adapting the reference as a mechanism for combining preference sensitivity with stable optimization.
icml-2025-alphadpo-adaptive-reward-margi.tldr: AlphaDPO adapts its reference distribution and preference margins to improve alignment while controlling changes between policy updates.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models can handle many tasks without task-specific training, but their zero-shot sentiment analysis performs poorly. This raises a practical question: do the models lack sentiment perception, or does the way they are asked fail to bring it out? The paper investigates this through demonstrations supplied in the input.

The study examines three aspects of in-context learning: how demonstrations are retrieved, how they are presented, and how they are distributed. It optimizes these factors and also identifies an inherent bias in the models’ sentiment predictions. The proposed strategies counteract that bias and complement one another, showing that the composition of the example context matters beyond simply including examples.

Across six multimodal sentiment datasets, the combined strategies deliver reported average accuracy improvements of 15.9% over zero-shot use and 11.2% over random demonstration selection. These findings support the authors’ conclusion that the tested models possess sentiment perception capabilities that weak prompting can obscure. They also make demonstration configuration a substantive part of the method, rather than a minor presentation choice.
icml-2025-an-empirical-study-on-configur.tldr: Carefully configuring in-context examples substantially improves multimodal sentiment analysis over zero-shot use and random demonstrations.

paragraphs: Sampling becomes difficult when a distribution has many dimensions and several separated regions of high probability. A useful sampler must explore those regions while remaining efficient and stable to train. Annealing Flow addresses this problem using continuous normalizing flows, with applications motivated by Bayesian inference and physics-based machine learning.

The method combines a dynamic optimal transport training objective with Wasserstein regularization and guidance from annealing procedures. These components shape how the flow moves probability toward the target distribution while encouraging exploration of its different modes. The contribution is the combination of transport-based training and annealing guidance for difficult distributions, rather than relying heavily on Monte Carlo assistance.

The authors report improved training efficiency and stability relative to recent normalizing-flow methods, with minimal reliance on Monte Carlo support. Experiments on challenging distributions and real-world datasets show superior performance against state-of-the-art methods, particularly in high-dimensional, multimodal settings. The paper also points to potential use in sampling least favorable distributions; that application is presented as a possibility rather than a general established capability.
icml-2025-annealing-flow-generative-mode.tldr: Annealing Flow combines continuous flows, optimal transport, and annealing to improve sampling of high-dimensional distributions with multiple modes.

paragraphs: Model compression often happens after training, once a large set of parameters has already been learned. BackSlash instead incorporates compression into training itself. The goal is to reduce parameter redundancy while allowing a flexible balance between model accuracy and complexity, making compactness part of the learning objective.

The approach uses rate-distortion optimization: it balances the cost of representing the model against the performance consequences of compression. A Lagrange multiplier controls this trade-off. This gives training an explicit incentive to find a less redundant parameter representation while preserving useful predictive behavior, rather than leaving all compression decisions until the model is finished.

Across the tested architectures and tasks, the authors report memory reductions of 60%–90% without accuracy loss and greater compression gains than post-training compression. They also report improved generalization with small multipliers and retained accuracy at pruning rates of 80%. Network simplification enables faster inference on edge devices. These findings describe several benefits observed in the experiments, with the generalization result specifically tied to the small-multiplier setting.
icml-2025-backslash-rate-constrained-opt.tldr: BackSlash makes compression part of training, reporting substantial memory savings without accuracy loss in its experiments.

paragraphs: Strong performance on some image-and-language tasks does not settle how deeply a model understands visual concepts. This paper examines that question using Bongard problems, classic visual puzzles requiring pattern recognition and abstract reasoning. The evaluation focuses on whether vision-language models can identify the concepts that distinguish the puzzle examples.

The tested models sometimes discover the relevant concepts and solve the puzzles, but they frequently fail. Even apparently elementary visual ideas, including simple spirals, cause difficulty. The authors also explicitly ask models to recognize the correct concepts. Continued failures in that setting suggest that the challenge extends beyond independently discovering which concept a puzzle is testing.

Comparisons with human performance reveal a substantial remaining gap in visual reasoning on these problems. The results suggest weaknesses in understanding elementary visual concepts and generalizing to unseen ones. Their significance is diagnostic: the evaluation separates occasional puzzle success from reliable conceptual competence and shows why broad impressions of advanced multimodal reasoning can miss persistent weaknesses on focused visual tests.
icml-2025-bongard-in-wonderland-visual-p.tldr: Bongard puzzle evaluations reveal persistent visual concept and reasoning failures in vision-language models, with a substantial gap from humans.

paragraphs: A system of collaborating vision-language agents can be vulnerable even when an attack initially succeeds against only one participant. That compromised agent can affect others, allowing the attack to spread through the group. Cowpox addresses this propagation problem, treating robustness as the ability to preserve system integrity during adversarial attacks.

The defense uses a distributed mechanism centered on a specially generated cure sample. This sample is distributed to agents before exposure to immunize them against the attack. The method aims to improve agents’ recovery rate while limiting the expected number of additional agents that become infected. Its focus therefore includes how a compromise moves through the collaborative system.

The authors provide theoretical robustness guarantees and empirical evidence that Cowpox is effective. The expected-infection formulation matters: the stated result concerns controlling propagation and improving robustness, rather than asserting that every possible attack is prevented. By connecting a preventive sample with a system-level spread mechanism, the paper offers a defense designed around the interactions that make multi-agent compromise especially consequential.
icml-2025-cowpox-towards-the-immunity-of.tldr: Cowpox distributes preventive cure samples to improve multi-agent robustness by limiting expected attack propagation.

paragraphs: An object detector that learns new categories can lose its ability to recognize old ones. Instead of treating the detector as a single unit, this paper examines the components of Faster R-CNN. It finds that forgetting is concentrated predominantly in the region-of-interest classifier, while the regressors remain robust across incremental stages.

This diagnosis motivates NSGP-RePRE. Its replay component stores two kinds of regional prototypes: coarse prototypes summarize each class’s semantic center, and finer prototypes represent variation within a class. Replaying both targets the classifier’s forgetting. A second component projects feature-extractor gradients into directions orthogonal to the old-input subspace, addressing misalignment between stored prototypes and features as learning continues.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on Pascal VOC and MS COCO under several settings. The significance is both practical and explanatory: a component-level analysis leads to a targeted combination of replay and constrained feature updates. The finding that regressors retain robustness also helps explain why applying the same forgetting remedy across every detector component may overlook where the main problem occurs.
icml-2025-demystifying-catastrophic-forg.tldr: NSGP-RePRE targets classifier-centered forgetting with regional prototype replay and gradient projection, improving incremental object detection.

paragraphs: When observations arrive late, a reinforcement learning agent must act using information about an environment that has already changed. It therefore needs an estimate of the current state. Existing forecasting approaches commonly advance through intermediate states one step at a time, creating a route for prediction errors to accumulate.

The Directly Forecasting Belief Transformer, or DFBT, predicts states directly from observations without recursively estimating each intervening state. The authors theoretically show that this reduces compounding errors relative to recursive forecasting and gives stronger performance guarantees. DFBT can also forecast sequences of states, which supports multi-step bootstrapping and improves the efficiency of learning.

Experiments using D4RL offline datasets show reduced error accumulation and strong prediction accuracy. A reinforcement learning method built around DFBT also substantially outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on MuJoCo. These results connect the forecasting change to both better state estimation and better learning outcomes. The central idea is that handling observation delay depends not only on forecasting accuracy, but also on whether the forecasting procedure repeatedly feeds its own errors forward.
icml-2025-directly-forecasting-belief-fo.tldr: DFBT directly forecasts states from delayed observations, reducing compounding prediction errors and improving reinforcement learning performance.

paragraphs: Inferring which of two variables causes the other often involves checking how well restricted causal models fit the observations. This paper introduces a different parameterization: treat the candidate cause as time in a dynamical system and describe the relationship through a causal velocity. Observations provide initial conditions for curves representing counterfactual outcomes.

Using measure transport, the authors establish a unique correspondence linking structural causal models and the generated distribution’s score function through causal velocity. They derive an objective that fits the velocity against this score, which can be estimated non-parametrically from observational data. The resulting discovery method extends beyond additive-noise and location-scale-noise models and does not require assumptions about noise distributions.

Simulations and benchmark experiments show positive results in settings where many existing methods fail. The objective can also help detect non-identifiability and model misspecification when the score is estimated well. That qualification is central: the paper explicitly studies sensitivity to score-estimation accuracy through ablations. The contribution broadens the model classes considered without claiming that observational causal direction is always identifiable.
icml-2025-distinguishing-cause-from-effe.tldr: Causal velocity models use dynamical systems and distribution scores to infer bivariate causal direction beyond familiar restricted noise models.

paragraphs: Whole slide image analysis can be formulated as multiple instance learning, where an example contains a collection of instances. These collections have inconsistent lengths, making them difficult to stack together for training. The paper identifies this mismatch as a source of both inefficiency and degraded performance in existing methods.

Distributed Parallel Gradient Stacking, or DPGS, addresses the stacking problem and is described as enabling lossless stacking of multiple instance learning data. The framework also includes Deep Model-Gradient Compression, which jointly compresses models and gradients to accelerate distributed training. The two components tackle related but distinct obstacles: handling uneven data collections and reducing the communication burden of training across distributed resources.

On Camelyon16 and TCGA-Lung, the authors report up to 31 times faster training, up to 99.2% less model communication at convergence, and up to 9.3% improved accuracy relative to the baseline. These are reported maximum gains, not uniform outcomes across every setting. The results indicate that resolving the stacking obstacle can accompany improvements in predictive performance as well as training efficiency.
icml-2025-distributed-parallel-gradient-.tldr: DPGS combines lossless multiple-instance data stacking with model-gradient compression to accelerate whole slide image training and improve accuracy.

paragraphs: A broadly pretrained time-series model may still perform worse than task-specific methods on a hospital’s private, imbalanced physiological data. At the same time, local computing resources may be insufficient for extensive adaptation. PhysioPFM addresses this combination of personalization needs, resource constraints, and concerns about training on sensitive medical data.

The framework first performs low-rank pre-training using public datasets. It then trains a generator from the resulting LoRA weights and uses local data to generate adaptation weights efficiently. This sequence transfers information from public-data adaptation into a mechanism for producing personalized model weights, reducing the need to conduct additional sensitive-data training for each adaptation.

The experiments show that integrating the generated models with a time-series foundation model improves performance and transferability while reducing additional training on sensitive data. The contribution is an adaptation workflow tailored to the constraints described, with weight generation taking a central role. The stated privacy-related benefit is reduced sensitive-data training; the abstract does not present that benefit as a formal privacy guarantee.
icml-2025-efficient-personalized-adaptat.tldr: PhysioPFM generates personalized adaptation weights for physiological time-series models, improving performance while reducing additional sensitive-data training.

paragraphs: Finding an audio recording that matches a description is different from identifying exactly when the described sound occurs. Existing audio-language models are strong at retrieval but weaker at this fine-grained timing task. Traditional sound event detectors can locate events precisely, but their predefined categories restrict which sounds they can recognize.

FLAM combines audio-language matching with frame-wise sound localization in an open vocabulary setting. Its training objective operates at the frame level and is designed to be memory-efficient and calibrated. Logit adjustment addresses misleading training correlations, including events that tend to occur together and imbalances among labels. For frame-wise supervision, the work uses diverse audio events, language-model-generated captions, and simulation.

Experiments and case studies show significant improvements in open-vocabulary localization while maintaining strong global retrieval and downstream performance. This means the timing improvements do not come with a reported collapse in whole-recording understanding. The paper’s contribution is to train the model for both what a sound means and where it appears in time, beyond a fixed event-category list.
icml-2025-flam-frame-wise-language-audio.tldr: FLAM improves open-vocabulary sound localization through calibrated frame-wise audio-language training while retaining strong retrieval performance.

paragraphs: Personalized diffusion models are often adapted from a pretrained model using a small image collection, then shared online. FineXtract investigates whether those released models expose the images used for adaptation. Successful extraction would demonstrate a data-leakage risk and could also provide evidence relevant to unauthorized use of training images.

The method approximates fine-tuning as a gradual movement from the original model’s learned distribution toward the adaptation data. It extrapolates using the models before and after fine-tuning to steer generation toward high-probability regions of the fine-tuning distribution. A clustering step then selects the most probable images from the generated candidates. This turns the difference between the two models into guidance for recovering adaptation examples.

Experiments include models fine-tuned on WikiArt and DreamBooth data, as well as checkpoints shared online. The authors report extracting approximately 20% of fine-tuning data in most cases, substantially exceeding baseline performance. That result indicates meaningful recoverability in the tested settings; it does not imply that all images, or the same fraction from every personalized model, can be recovered.
icml-2025-leveraging-model-guidance-to-e.tldr: FineXtract uses differences between pretrained and personalized diffusion models to recover approximately 20% of fine-tuning images in most tested cases.

paragraphs: Transformers can treat information differently depending on where it appears in a sequence. This paper develops a graph-theoretic explanation of such position biases across multiple attention layers. It represents attention masks as directed graphs, allowing the analysis to track how a token’s position shapes its access to contextual information.

The first finding is that causal masking inherently favors earlier positions: deeper layers attend to increasingly contextualized representations of earlier tokens. The second concerns the interaction with relative positional mechanisms, including decay masks and rotary positional encoding. Although these introduce distance-based decay within individual attention maps, their combined behavior over layers creates a trade-off between long-range decay and the accumulating importance of early positions.

Controlled numerical experiments support the theoretical findings and reproduce position biases observed in real-world language models. The main lesson is that a single attention map does not capture the full positional effect of an architecture. Bias emerges from interactions among masking, positional encoding, and depth, giving architectural analysis a way to reason about effects that accumulate across layers.
icml-2025-on-the-emergence-of-position-b.tldr: A graph-based analysis explains how causal masks, positional encodings, and depth jointly create transformer position biases.

paragraphs: Open-world object detection requires recognizing potential objects beyond the categories a detector already knows, then learning new categories over time. Existing attribute-based approaches depend on language-model descriptions whose accuracy affects detection. OW-VAP instead operates independently of a large language model and needs only minimal object descriptions.

Its Visual Attribute Parser examines image regions and compares their parsed attributes with object descriptions to judge whether they could contain objects. Training also draws on potential objects in background regions, helping the parser recognize objects that lack labels. Because background can be mistakenly treated as foreground, a probabilistic soft-label assignment mechanism addresses the resulting conflicts during optimization.

On the open-world detection benchmark, the authors report improvements of 13 in U-Recall and 8 in U-AP over existing state-of-the-art methods. They also report approaching the detector’s upper limit for unknown-object recall. These findings support visual attribute parsing as a way to strengthen unknown detection while reducing dependence on generated category descriptions. The soft-label component addresses the ambiguity introduced by learning from potentially unlabeled objects.
icml-2025-ow-vap-visual-attribute-parsin.tldr: OW-VAP detects unknown objects through visual attribute parsing and probabilistic labels, improving open-world detection without an LLM.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks offer a neural approach to solving partial differential equations, but building an effective model requires both domain knowledge and deep learning expertise. Existing practice often involves extensive manual experiments followed by heuristic tuning rules. PINNsAgent aims to automate this surrogation process using large language models.

The framework combines two mechanisms. Physics-Guided Knowledge Replay transfers knowledge from already solved equations to similar problems. Memory Tree Reasoning explores the space of possible PINN architectures. Together, these components connect reusable problem-solving experience with architecture search, addressing both how earlier solutions can inform a new problem and how candidate network designs can be explored.

The authors evaluate PINNsAgent on 14 benchmark partial differential equations and report effective automation with significantly improved solution accuracy. The result supports using an LLM-centered framework to coordinate the design of physics-informed neural surrogates. Its practical contribution is to reduce the reliance on manually accumulated tuning experience while using similarities among equations to make previous work useful for subsequent problems.
icml-2025-pinnsagent-automated-pde-surro.tldr: PINNsAgent combines knowledge replay and architecture search to automate neural PDE surrogation and improve solution accuracy.

paragraphs: Chain-of-thought reasoning and self-training both reuse information produced by a model to reduce uncertainty over successive steps. This paper takes that shared objective as a starting point for a new reasoning framework. The aim is to make iterative reasoning more productive, rather than assuming that additional reasoning automatically improves an answer.

The framework has two components. A task-specific prompt module improves the initial reasoning process, while an adaptive iteration module refines what follows. The latter addresses two identified problems in prior chain-of-thought approaches: continuing to reason excessively and generating successive iterations that are highly similar. These problems matter because repeated model output can consume computation without providing much new information.

Extensive experiments show significant advantages in both reasoning performance and computational efficiency. The reported combination supports the idea that better use of model-generated information can improve answers while reducing unproductive reasoning. The contribution is a framework that treats the initial prompt and subsequent refinement as connected design choices, with iteration adapted to address redundancy and over-reasoning.
icml-2025-rethinking-chain-of-thought-fr.tldr: A self-training-inspired chain-of-thought framework improves reasoning and efficiency through task-specific prompting and adaptive refinement.

paragraphs: DINO and DINOv2 learn useful visual representations from unlabeled images, but their training depends on many carefully tuned design choices. A central concern is representation collapse, where learned features cease to provide useful distinctions. This paper asks whether an explicit training objective can replace much of the complexity used to prevent that outcome.

The authors add a coding-rate term to the loss and remove most of the empirically motivated peculiarities in the original pre-training pipelines. The resulting variants are called SimDINO and SimDINOv2. The proposed simplification puts collapse prevention directly into the objective, reducing dependence on a collection of interacting pipeline choices and hyperparameter settings.

The simplified models are reported to be more robust to architectural and hyperparameter choices while learning representations that perform better on downstream tasks. The authors describe this as a Pareto improvement over the corresponding DINO models: simplification accompanies improved representation quality. The broader finding is that making a training requirement explicit can, in this setting, improve both practical robustness and the usefulness of learned features.
icml-2025-simplifying-dino-via-coding-ra.tldr: SimDINO replaces much of DINO’s training complexity with coding-rate regularization, improving robustness and downstream representation quality.

paragraphs: Video diffusion transformers spend substantial computation on full attention across space and time. Its cost grows quadratically with context length, contributing to long generation times. Sparse VideoGen aims to accelerate inference without training by exploiting the fact that only certain attention connections dominate each head’s output.

The paper identifies two dynamic patterns. Spatial heads primarily use spatially related tokens within a frame, while temporal heads primarily use tokens related across frames. An online profiling strategy detects these patterns and predicts head types during inference. Hardware-efficient tensor layout transformations and customized kernels then turn the identified sparsity into computational savings.

The authors report end-to-end speedups of up to 2.28 times on CogVideoX-v1.5 and 2.33 times on HunyuanVideo while preserving generation quality. These are maximum reported gains for the evaluated models. The contribution connects an observation about attention behavior with implementation choices needed for practical acceleration: identifying sparse connections alone is only part of the method, alongside arranging and executing the remaining computation efficiently.
icml-2025-sparse-video-gen-accelerating-.tldr: Sparse VideoGen exploits dynamic spatial and temporal attention sparsity for training-free video generation speedups while preserving quality.

paragraphs: Graph models need to generalize when the structure of connections changes, not only when individual data values change. This paper focuses on such topological shifts, an aspect the authors argue has received insufficient attention. AdvDIFFormer is a graph transformer designed around this structural generalization problem.

The model is derived from advective diffusion equations, which describe a continuous message-passing process involving both observed and latent graph structures. This physics-inspired formulation supplies the basis for the authors’ theoretical analysis. They show that AdvDIFFormer can provably control generalization error under topological shifts, a guarantee they contrast with what graph diffusion models can provide.

Experiments show superior predictive performance across information networks, molecular screening, and protein interactions. These results accompany the theoretical contribution with evidence from several graph applications. The distinction in the theory concerns the availability of an error-control guarantee; it does not mean that every diffusion-based graph model must fail on every changed graph. The paper makes changing connectivity an explicit part of model design and generalization analysis.
icml-2025-supercharging-graph-transforme.tldr: AdvDIFFormer uses advective diffusion to improve graph prediction and provide theoretical control of generalization error under topological shifts.

paragraphs: Selecting supervised fine-tuning data requires attention to both quality and diversity. Favoring only one can produce a less effective training subset. GraphFilter frames the selection task as a set cover problem, making coverage of the dataset’s content part of the decision about which examples to retain.

The method constructs a bipartite graph linking sentences to their constituent n-grams. It assigns each sentence a priority that multiplies quality and diversity measures, then repeatedly chooses the highest-priority sentence. After each choice, covered n-grams are removed and priorities are recalculated. Consequently, a sentence’s value changes as the selected subset grows: content already covered affects what is useful to add next.

Tests with three model backbones across six benchmarks show better model performance and computational efficiency than nine existing baselines. Further analysis supports the design choices and highlights the value of instruction diversity. It also examines how quality and diversity interact at different subset sizes, reinforcing that effective selection depends on both individual examples and the composition of the developing collection.
icml-2025-the-best-of-both-worlds-bridgi.tldr: GraphFilter dynamically balances example quality and content coverage to select more effective and computationally efficient fine-tuning subsets.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can produce a plausible explanation that does not support its own answer. Such misalignment contributes to inconsistent reasoning and incorrect visual question answering. Self-Rationale Calibration, or SRC, trains models to improve the relationship between the rationale they give and the answer they ultimately produce.

SRC first uses lightweight rationale fine-tuning so the model naturally generates a rationale before its answer, without needing an explicit prompt to request that format. It then searches for diverse candidate responses for each sample. A tailored model called R-Scorer evaluates pairs of candidates for rationale quality and factual consistency, and a confidence-weighted process turns those judgments into preference training data.

The framework iteratively calibrates alignment through preference fine-tuning. Across multiple benchmarks, the authors report significant improvements in perception, reasoning, and generalization. The contribution goes beyond requiring explanatory text: candidate rationales and their consistency help determine which responses the model learns to prefer. The reported results support treating rationale-answer alignment as a training objective that can improve broader visual-language performance.
icml-2025-towards-rationale-answer-align.tldr: SRC scores and curates rationale-based preferences to improve consistency between vision-language models’ explanations and answers.

paragraphs: Automatic algorithm selection tries to choose the best-performing algorithm before running it. Common approaches rely on correlations between problem descriptors and observed performance. This paper instead asks which algorithm characteristics are suited to problems with particular features, aiming to make selection more explainable and less vulnerable to biased data.

The proposed framework uses a directed acyclic graph to describe that relationship. It models algorithm features conditioned on problem features and reconstructs the characteristics of an optimal algorithm. The final choice uses differences between those reconstructed characteristics and the features of rejected algorithms. This provides a finer-grained basis for selection than treating the outcome solely as an association between descriptors and performance.

The authors report enhanced robustness to changes in marginal distributions. They also show that the learned graph supports explanations of the model’s overall behavior, while counterfactual calculations explain individual decisions. The stated robustness concerns this particular kind of distribution change. The contribution connects selection, reconstruction, and explanation through one account of how problem properties relate to suitable algorithm properties.
icml-2025-towards-robustness-and-explain.tldr: A graph-based algorithm selector reconstructs suitable algorithm features to improve robustness to marginal shifts and explain its decisions.

paragraphs: Compressing a neural network’s weight matrices can remove noise as well as reduce model size. The challenge is deciding which parts of the matrix’s eigenvalue structure represent useful information. This paper introduces the Population Double Bulk model to describe that structure more generally than the existing Population Unit Bulk model.

Using the new model and random matrix theory, the authors develop PDBLS to locate a boundary between noisy eigenvalues and informative structure. A subsequent PDB Noise-Filtering algorithm uses that distinction to reduce matrix rank for compression. The approach links a statistical description of the learned weights to a concrete rule for deciding which components to remove.

Experiments show that the PDB model fits empirical weight eigenvalue distributions better than the PUB model. The resulting compressed matrices have lower rank at the same test accuracy. In some cases with noisy labels, compression also improves generalization. That last benefit is explicitly conditional: the findings establish occasional gains in noisy-label settings, alongside the broader reported ability to obtain lower-rank matrices without sacrificing test accuracy.
icml-2025-weight-matrices-compression-ba.tldr: The PDB model improves identification of noisy weight components, enabling lower-rank compression at the same test accuracy.
